name: Purple Brown
lede: Purple brown is a dark, reddish brown with a violet cast; as a paint name it described the deepest shade of an artificial iron oxide.

sections.title: A name from iron oxide
sections.body: Heaton's 1928 paint handbook uses purple brown for the deepest shade of artificial iron oxide [1]. The phrase is probably related to a purple brown calx of iron, a description of colcothar (roasted iron sulfate) in an English treatise of 1795 [2]. Harley notes that colcothar vitriol is listed as a color name in Atkinson in 1794, described there as a bright, light purple [2]. Terry in 1893 calls colcothar a fancy name for a kind of iron oxide pigment, and says it was synthetic [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Our library gives this color three sources: the xkcd survey, ISCC-NBS block 43 and Ridgway's 1912 atlas, plate XII [3]. Ridgway's name for the same color is Violet Carmine, only 1.6 units away [3]. Its nearest everyday name is [[mahogany]], 10.8 units away, and close neighbors include [[maroon]], [[sepia]] and [[plum]] [3]. The phrase also turns up as a modern paint label: Baty's chart of paint ranges lists a Purple Brown among the decorator colors of one maker, Little Greene [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In the archive, 162 of 23,781 paintings carry this brown, mostly in shadows: 57 per cent of the matched area sits in the darkest zone [5]. Albrecht Dürer and Henri Matisse each show it in 3 works, about nine times the archive rate [5]. The words *purple brown* peak in printed English around 1901 [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so treat the counts as approximate [5].
